/-!
# Hyperbolic Number Theory: The Ford-Circle Tessellation of the Modular Group

The modular group `Γ = PSL(2, ℤ)` acts on the hyperbolic upper half-plane, and the
orbit of the horocycle at `∞` produces the classical *Ford circles*: for each reduced
fraction `p/q` the circle in the upper half-plane tangent to the real axis at `p/q`
with Euclidean radius `1/(2q²)`.  These circles are the horocyclic "cusps" of the
modular tessellation; their tangency graph is exactly the **Farey graph**.

This file makes precise the sense in which — echoing the research theme "primes are
geometric objects" — the arithmetic relation of *unimodularity* between two fractions
is identical to the *geometric* relation of *tangency* between their Ford circles.

## Main results

* `ford_gap_identity` — the exact algebraic identity
  `centerDistSq - (r₁+r₂)² = ((ps-qr)² - 1) / (q²s²)`, the arithmetic-geometric bridge.
* `ford_tangent_iff_unimodular` — **two Ford circles are (externally) tangent iff the
  two fractions are unimodular neighbours** `|ps - qr| = 1`.
* `ford_circles_disjoint` — distinct Ford circles never overlap: their centres are
  always at least the sum of the radii apart (the tessellation is a genuine packing).
* `mediant_tangent_left` / `mediant_tangent_right` — the **Stern–Brocot mediant**
  `(p+r)/(q+s)` of two tangent Ford circles is tangent to both, recursively generating
  new vertices of the tessellation, and its coordinates are automatically coprime.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): In the Poincaré/upper-half-plane model of hyperbolic
geometry the vertices of the modular tessellation are the tangency points of Ford
circles.  Conjecture: two Ford circles touch *exactly* when the underlying fractions
`p/q`, `r/s` satisfy the unimodular (Farey-neighbour) relation `ps - qr = ±1`.  A
sharper, surprising claim: the *same* algebraic quantity `(ps-qr)² - 1 ≥ 0` forces the
circles to never overlap, so the modular tessellation is a rigid circle *packing* with
no slack — tangency is the extremal case of disjointness.

Experiment (Experimenter): Computed `(ps-qr)` and the sign of
`centerDistSq - (r₁+r₂)²` for all fractions with `q, s ≤ 6`.  Every tangent pair had
`|ps-qr| = 1`; every non-adjacent pair had `|ps-qr| ≥ 2` and strictly positive gap.
The single identity `centerDistSq - (r₁+r₂)² = ((ps-qr)²-1)/(q²s²)` reproduces every
case, so the whole phenomenon is one polynomial identity plus positivity of `q²s²`.

Analysis (Analyst): The heart is `ford_gap_identity`, provable by `field_simp; ring`.
Everything else is positivity bookkeeping (`(ps-qr)² ≥ 1` for distinct fractions) plus
the elementary mediant computations `p(q+s) - q(p+r) = ps - qr`.  No transcendental
input is needed — the hyperbolic geometry of the cusps is entirely captured by the
integer determinant `ps - qr`.

Critique (Critic): "Tangent" is stated via *squared* distance `centerDistSq = (r₁+r₂)²`
to avoid `Real.sqrt`; since distances and radii are nonnegative this is equivalent to
the honest metric statement `dist = r₁ + r₂`, recorded in `ford_tangent_iff_dist`.
The disjointness theorem needs `ps - qr ≠ 0`, i.e. the fractions are genuinely distinct
points of `ℚ`; that hypothesis is necessary (a circle is tangent to itself).
-/

namespace FordTessellation

open scoped BigOperators

noncomputable section

/-! ## Ford circles -/

/-- Euclidean `x`-coordinate of the centre of the Ford circle of the fraction `p/q`:
it is tangent to the real axis at `p/q`. -/
def fordX (p q : ℤ) : ℝ := (p : ℝ) / q

/-- Euclidean `y`-coordinate of the centre of the Ford circle of `p/q`, equal to its
radius `1/(2q²)`. -/
def fordY (q : ℤ) : ℝ := 1 / (2 * (q : ℝ) ^ 2)

/-- Euclidean radius of the Ford circle of `p/q`. -/
def fordR (q : ℤ) : ℝ := 1 / (2 * (q : ℝ) ^ 2)

/-- Squared Euclidean distance between the centres of the Ford circles of `p/q`, `r/s`. -/
def centerDistSq (p q r s : ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (fordX p q - fordX r s) ^ 2 + (fordY q - fordY s) ^ 2

theorem fordR_pos {q : ℤ} (hq : q ≠ 0) : 0 < fordR q := by
  have hq' : (q : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hq
  unfold fordR
  positivity

/-- **The arithmetic–geometric gap identity.**  The difference between the squared
centre-distance of two Ford circles and the square of the sum of their radii is a pure
function of the integer determinant `ps - qr`:
`centerDistSq - (r₁ + r₂)² = ((ps - qr)² - 1) / (q²s²)`. -/
theorem ford_gap_identity (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0) :
    centerDistSq p q r s - (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2
      = (((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) / ((q : ℝ) ^ 2 * (s : ℝ) ^ 2) := by
  have hq' : (q : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hq
  have hs' : (s : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hs
  unfold centerDistSq fordX fordY fordR
  push_cast
  field_simp
  ring

/-- An integer squares to `1` iff it is `±1`. -/
theorem sq_eq_one_iff_int (n : ℤ) : n ^ 2 = 1 ↔ n = 1 ∨ n = -1 := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    have : (n - 1) * (n + 1) = 0 := by ring_nf; linarith [h]
    rcases mul_eq_zero.mp this with h1 | h2
    · left; omega
    · right; omega
  · rintro (rfl | rfl) <;> ring

/-! ## Main theorem: tangency ⇔ unimodularity -/

/-- **Ford circles are tangent iff the fractions are unimodular neighbours.**
Two Ford circles of `p/q` and `r/s` (with `q, s ≠ 0`) are externally tangent — their
centre-distance equals the sum of the radii — precisely when `ps - qr = ±1`, i.e. the
fractions are Farey neighbours. -/
theorem ford_tangent_iff_unimodular (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0) :
    centerDistSq p q r s = (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2 ↔
      (p * s - q * r = 1 ∨ p * s - q * r = -1) := by
  have hq' : (q : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hq
  have hs' : (s : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hs
  have hden : ((q : ℝ) ^ 2 * (s : ℝ) ^ 2) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  rw [← sub_eq_zero, ford_gap_identity p q r s hq hs, div_eq_zero_iff]
  constructor
  · rintro (h | h)
    · have hone : (((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ)) ^ 2 = 1 := by linarith
      have hint : ((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 = (((p * s - q * r) ^ 2 : ℤ) : ℝ) := by
        push_cast; ring
      rw [hint] at hone
      have hZ : ((p * s - q * r) ^ 2 : ℤ) = 1 := by exact_mod_cast hone
      exact (sq_eq_one_iff_int _).mp hZ
    · exact absurd h hden
  · intro h
    left
    have hZ : ((p * s - q * r) ^ 2 : ℤ) = 1 := (sq_eq_one_iff_int _).mpr h
    have hR : ((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 = 1 := by exact_mod_cast hZ
    linarith

/-- **The tessellation is a packing.**  Distinct Ford circles never overlap: whenever
the fractions are different points of `ℚ` (`ps - qr ≠ 0`), the centre-distance is at
least the sum of the radii, with equality exactly in the tangent (unimodular) case. -/
theorem ford_circles_disjoint (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0)
    (hne : p * s - q * r ≠ 0) :
    (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2 ≤ centerDistSq p q r s := by
  have hq' : (q : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hq
  have hs' : (s : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by exact_mod_cast hs
  have hge1 : (1 : ℤ) ≤ (p * s - q * r) ^ 2 := by
    have hnz : (p * s - q * r) ^ 2 ≠ 0 := pow_ne_zero _ hne
    have hnn : (0 : ℤ) ≤ (p * s - q * r) ^ 2 := sq_nonneg _
    omega
  have hgap : 0 ≤ (((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 - 1) / ((q : ℝ) ^ 2 * (s : ℝ) ^ 2) := by
    apply div_nonneg
    · have h1 : (1 : ℝ) ≤ ((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 := by
        have hc : (1 : ℝ) ≤ (((p * s - q * r) ^ 2 : ℤ) : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hge1
        rw [show ((p * s - q * r : ℤ) : ℝ) ^ 2 = (((p * s - q * r) ^ 2 : ℤ) : ℝ) by
          push_cast; ring]
        exact hc
      linarith
    · positivity
  have hid := ford_gap_identity p q r s hq hs
  linarith [hid, hgap]

/-- The honest metric restatement of tangency: since all quantities are nonnegative,
`centerDistSq = (r₁+r₂)²` is equivalent to the Euclidean distance between centres being
exactly the sum of the radii. -/
theorem ford_tangent_iff_dist (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0) :
    centerDistSq p q r s = (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2 ↔
      Real.sqrt (centerDistSq p q r s) = fordR q + fordR s := by
  have hR : 0 ≤ fordR q + fordR s := by
    have h1 := fordR_pos hq; have h2 := fordR_pos hs; linarith
  constructor
  · intro h
    rw [h, Real.sqrt_sq hR]
  · intro h
    have hnn : 0 ≤ centerDistSq p q r s := by
      unfold centerDistSq; positivity
    have hsq := Real.sq_sqrt hnn
    rw [h] at hsq
    linarith [hsq]

/-! ## Stern–Brocot mediants: recursive generation of tessellation vertices -/

/-- Mediant determinant, left: `p·(q+s) - q·(p+r) = ps - qr`. -/
theorem mediant_det_left (p q r s : ℤ) :
    p * (q + s) - q * (p + r) = p * s - q * r := by ring

/-- Mediant determinant, right: `(p+r)·s - (q+s)·r = ps - qr`. -/
theorem mediant_det_right (p q r s : ℤ) :
    (p + r) * s - (q + s) * r = p * s - q * r := by ring

/-- **The mediant Ford circle is tangent to the left parent.**  If `p/q` and `r/s` are
unimodular neighbours, then the Ford circle of the mediant `(p+r)/(q+s)` is tangent to
that of `p/q`. -/
theorem mediant_tangent_left (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hqs : q + s ≠ 0)
    (h : p * s - q * r = 1 ∨ p * s - q * r = -1) :
    centerDistSq p q (p + r) (q + s) = (fordR q + fordR (q + s)) ^ 2 := by
  rw [ford_tangent_iff_unimodular p q (p + r) (q + s) hq hqs, mediant_det_left]
  exact h

/-- **The mediant Ford circle is tangent to the right parent.** -/
theorem mediant_tangent_right (p q r s : ℤ) (hs : s ≠ 0) (hqs : q + s ≠ 0)
    (h : p * s - q * r = 1 ∨ p * s - q * r = -1) :
    centerDistSq (p + r) (q + s) r s = (fordR (q + s) + fordR s) ^ 2 := by
  rw [ford_tangent_iff_unimodular (p + r) (q + s) r s hqs hs, mediant_det_right]
  exact h

/-- **Mediant coordinates are automatically coprime.**  Unimodularity of the parents
forces the mediant `(p+r)/(q+s)` to be already in lowest terms — so each mediant step
produces a genuinely new reduced fraction (vertex) of the tessellation. -/
theorem mediant_coprime (p q r s : ℤ)
    (h : p * s - q * r = 1 ∨ p * s - q * r = -1) :
    IsCoprime (p + r) (q + s) := by
  rcases h with h | h
  · exact ⟨s, -r, by linear_combination h⟩
  · exact ⟨-s, r, by linear_combination -h⟩

end

end FordTessellation

are the tangency points of Ford circles.  Here we prove that this whole structure is
`Γ`-**equivariant**:

* `modular_action_det` — the fractional-linear action of any `g ∈ SL(2, ℤ)` on a pair
  of column vectors *preserves the determinant* `ps - qr`.  This is the exact sense in
  which the group action "respects the arithmetic".
* `modular_preserves_farey` — consequently `Γ` maps Farey neighbours to Farey neighbours
  (reusing the catalog predicate `IsFareyNeighbor`).
* `ford_tangent_iff_fareyNeighbor` — the geometric tangency of Basic.lean is literally
  the catalog's arithmetic Farey-neighbour relation.
* `modular_preserves_ford_tangency` — therefore `Γ` maps tangent Ford circles to tangent
  Ford circles: the tessellation is a `Γ`-invariant object, i.e. the modular group is a
  genuine symmetry group of "hyperbolic arithmetic".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): If the Ford tessellation encodes the arithmetic of the cusps,
then the modular group `SL(2, ℤ)`, which permutes the cusps by fractional-linear maps,
must act as a symmetry of the tessellation.  Concretely: the adjacency relation
("tangent Ford circles" = "unimodular fractions") should be preserved by every
`g ∈ SL(2, ℤ)`.  Surprising sharpening: not merely the *relation* `|ps-qr| = 1` but the
*signed determinant* `ps - qr` itself is an exact invariant of the action.

Experiment (Experimenter): For `g = S` (`z ↦ -1/z`) and `g = T` (`z ↦ z+1`) and several
Farey pairs, computed the transformed pairs and their determinants: the value `ps - qr`
was reproduced identically every time.  The determinant multiplicativity
`det(g · M) = det g · det M` with `det g = 1` explains it in one line.

Analysis (Analyst): The core is the polynomial identity
`(ap+bq)(cr+ds) - (cp+dq)(ar+bs) = (ad-bc)(ps-qr)`, closed by `ring`, combined with
`MobiusMap.det_one`.  Everything geometric then follows from
`FordTessellation.ford_tangent_iff_unimodular`, so no new analysis is required — the
symmetry is purely algebraic.  The only side condition is that the images keep nonzero
denominators (a cusp may be sent to `∞`), which we carry as explicit hypotheses.

Critique (Critic): `IsFareyNeighbor` and `MobiusMap` are *imported* from the catalog, so
these theorems genuinely extend the existing thread rather than re-deriving it.  The
tangency ⇔ Farey-neighbour bridge (`ford_tangent_iff_fareyNeighbor`) is an honest `iff`
between a geometric statement (Euclidean distances of circles) and an arithmetic one
(a determinant equation), not a definitional rewrite.
-/

namespace FordTessellation

open scoped BigOperators

/-- The fractional-linear action of a modular matrix on a column vector `(p, q)`,
representing the cusp `p/q`.  This is `(p, q) ↦ (a·p + b·q, c·p + d·q)`. -/
def act (g : MobiusMap) (p q : ℤ) : ℤ × ℤ :=
  (g.a * p + g.b * q, g.c * p + g.d * q)

@[simp] theorem act_fst (g : MobiusMap) (p q : ℤ) :
    (act g p q).1 = g.a * p + g.b * q := rfl

@[simp] theorem act_snd (g : MobiusMap) (p q : ℤ) :
    (act g p q).2 = g.c * p + g.d * q := rfl

/-- **The modular action preserves the determinant `ps - qr`.**  For any
`g ∈ SL(2, ℤ)`, applying `g` to both cusps `p/q` and `r/s` leaves the integer
`ps - qr` unchanged.  This is the arithmetic-invariance heart of the equivariance. -/
theorem modular_action_det (g : MobiusMap) (p q r s : ℤ) :
    (act g p q).1 * (act g r s).2 - (act g p q).2 * (act g r s).1
      = p * s - q * r := by
  simp only [act_fst, act_snd]
  have hdet := g.det_one
  linear_combination (p * s - q * r) * hdet

/-- **The modular group maps Farey neighbours to Farey neighbours** (catalog predicate
`IsFareyNeighbor`).  A direct corollary of determinant invariance. -/
theorem modular_preserves_farey (g : MobiusMap) (p q r s : ℤ)
    (h : IsFareyNeighbor p q r s) :
    IsFareyNeighbor (act g p q).1 (act g p q).2 (act g r s).1 (act g r s).2 := by
  unfold IsFareyNeighbor at h ⊢
  rw [modular_action_det g p q r s]
  exact h

/-- **Geometric tangency equals arithmetic Farey-adjacency.**  The Euclidean tangency of
two Ford circles (`Basic.ford_tangent_iff_unimodular`) is exactly the catalog's
`IsFareyNeighbor` relation between the fractions. -/
theorem ford_tangent_iff_fareyNeighbor (p q r s : ℤ) (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0) :
    centerDistSq p q r s = (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2 ↔ IsFareyNeighbor p q r s := by
  rw [ford_tangent_iff_unimodular p q r s hq hs]
  rfl

/-- **The modular group is a symmetry of the Ford tessellation.**  If `p/q` and `r/s`
have tangent Ford circles, then so do their images under any `g ∈ SL(2, ℤ)` (whenever
those images have nonzero denominators, i.e. neither cusp is sent to `∞`). -/
theorem modular_preserves_ford_tangency (g : MobiusMap) (p q r s : ℤ)
    (hq : q ≠ 0) (hs : s ≠ 0)
    (hq' : (act g p q).2 ≠ 0) (hs' : (act g r s).2 ≠ 0)
    (htan : centerDistSq p q r s = (fordR q + fordR s) ^ 2) :
    centerDistSq (act g p q).1 (act g p q).2 (act g r s).1 (act g r s).2
      = (fordR (act g p q).2 + fordR (act g r s).2) ^ 2 := by
  rw [ford_tangent_iff_unimodular _ _ _ _ hq' hs']
  have hfarey : IsFareyNeighbor p q r s :=
    (ford_tangent_iff_fareyNeighbor p q r s hq hs).mp htan
  have := modular_preserves_farey g p q r s hfarey
  unfold IsFareyNeighbor at this
  exact this

/-- Sanity instance: the generator `T : z ↦ z + 1` sends the tangent pair `0/1, 1/1`
to the tangent pair `1/1, 2/1`, exhibiting the equivariance concretely. -/
theorem modular_action_det_T_example :
    (act MobiusMap.T 0 1).1 * (act MobiusMap.T 1 1).2
      - (act MobiusMap.T 0 1).2 * (act MobiusMap.T 1 1).1 = 0 * 1 - 1 * 1 :=
  modular_action_det MobiusMap.T 0 1 1 1

end FordTessellation

# Computational Evidence — Ford-Circle Tessellation of the Modular Group

All computations below were run over exact integers/rationals (no floating point),
matching the quantities that appear in the formal statements.

## 1. The gap identity, checked on small cases

For fractions `p/q` and `r/s`, the formal identity proved in `Basic.lean` is

```
centerDistSq − (r₁+r₂)²  =  ((ps − qr)² − 1) / (q²s²).
```

Because `q²s² > 0`, the **sign** of the geometric gap `centerDistSq − (r₁+r₂)²`
equals the sign of the integer `(ps − qr)² − 1`. Sample table (`d = ps − qr`):

| p/q | r/s | d = ps−qr | d²−1 | meaning |
|-----|-----|-----------|------|---------|
| 0/1 | 1/1 | −1 | 0 | tangent |
| 0/1 | 1/2 | −1 | 0 | tangent |
| 0/1 | 1/3 | −1 | 0 | tangent |
| 0/1 | 2/3 | −2 | 3 | disjoint |
| 0/1 | 3/4 | −3 | 8 | disjoint |
| 1/1 | 1/3 | 2 | 3 | disjoint |
| 1/1 | 2/3 | 1 | 0 | tangent |
| 1/1 | 1/4 | 3 | 8 | disjoint |

Every row with `|d| = 1` has gap `= 0` (tangency); every row with `|d| ≥ 2` has gap
`> 0` (disjoint interiors). No row ever gave a negative gap — consistent with the
theorem `ford_circles_disjoint` (Ford circles never overlap).

## 2. Counterexample hunt

Over the fraction sample `{0/1, 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, 2/3, 1/4, 3/4, 2/5, 3/5}` (all 72
ordered distinct pairs) we searched for:

* a **tangent** pair with `|ps − qr| ≠ 1` — none found;
* a pair with **negative** gap (overlapping circles) — none found;
* the number of tangent (`d² − 1 = 0`) pairs — **30**, exactly the pairs with `|d| = 1`.

No counterexample to `ford_tangent_iff_unimodular` or to `ford_circles_disjoint` was
found.

## 3. Mediants (Stern–Brocot / Farey generation)

Starting from the tangent pair `0/1, 1/1` (`d = −1`), repeated insertion of mediants
reproduces the Stern–Brocot / Farey tree:

```
0/1 , 1/1
0/1 , 1/2 , 1/1
0/1 , 1/3 , 1/2 , 2/3 , 1/1
0/1 , 1/4 , 1/3 , 2/5 , 1/2 , 3/5 , 2/3 , 3/4 , 1/1
```

At every step each newly inserted mediant `(p+r)/(q+s)` satisfies `|det| = 1` with both
neighbours (formalised by `mediant_tangent_left`, `mediant_tangent_right`) and is
automatically in lowest terms (`mediant_coprime`).

## 4. Modular action (equivariance)

The generator `T : z ↦ z + 1` acts as `(p, q) ↦ (p + q, q)`. On the tangent pair
`0/1, 1/1` it gives `1/1, 2/1`, and the determinant is preserved:
`det(0/1, 1/1) = −1 = det(1/1, 2/1)`. The generator `S : z ↦ −1/z` acts as
`(p, q) ↦ (−q, p)`; on `0/1, 1/1` it gives `(−1)/0, (−1)/1`, i.e. `∞` and `−1/1`, with
determinant again `−1`. This matches `modular_action_det` (determinant is an exact
invariant) and, away from the cusp `∞`, `modular_preserves_ford_tangency`.

## 5. OEIS connections

* Denominators appearing along the Stern–Brocot mediant construction reproduce the
  Stern diatomic sequence **A002487** (`1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 1, 4, …`).
* The number of fractions in the Farey sequence `F_n` is **A005728**; its successive
  differences are values of Euler's totient (**A000010**), already present in the
  catalog thread via `eulerTotientSum`.

# Future Directions — Arithmetic on the Poincaré Disk

The results of this cycle establish that the adjacency structure of the modular
tessellation is governed by a single integer determinant `ps − qr`: two horocyclic
cusps touch exactly when their determinant is a unit, the tessellation is a rigid
packing with no slack, mediants regenerate the whole structure, and the modular group
acts as an exact symmetry preserving the determinant. These findings suggest the
following bold, testable directions.

## 1. The determinant is the *only* invariant of cusp pairs

**Conjecture.** Two ordered pairs of cusps are related by an orientation-preserving
symmetry of the tessellation if and only if they have the same signed determinant
`ps − qr`. In particular, the symmetry group acts transitively on the set of tangent
(determinant `±1`) pairs.

*The key insight is* that determinant preservation, proved here to be necessary, is
also sufficient: given any two pairs with equal determinant one can build an explicit
group element carrying one to the other by solving a single linear system with a
unimodular constraint.

*Why now?* We have just isolated the determinant as the exact conserved quantity of the
action; the natural next question — whether it is a *complete* invariant — is now sharply
posed and directly checkable on the same finite samples already used as evidence.

## 2. A curvature-corrected counting law for tangency points

**Conjecture.** The number of tangency points of the tessellation whose two cusps both
have denominator at most `Q` grows like `C · Q² + O(Q log Q)`, with the leading constant
`C` expressible through `ζ(2) = π²/6`.

*The key insight is* that each tangency point is a unimodular pair `(p/q, r/s)` with
bounded denominators, so counting them is counting coprime lattice configurations in a
box — a problem whose main term is dictated by the density of coprime pairs, `6/π²`.

*Why now?* The equivalence "tangency = unimodularity" turns a genuinely geometric
counting problem into an elementary lattice-point count, removing the transcendental
obstacles that make the naïve "hyperbolic prime number theorem" ill-posed.

## 3. Tangency chains and continued fractions

**Conjecture.** The minimal number of mediant steps required to reach a reduced fraction
`p/q` from the seed pair `0/1, 1/1` equals the sum of the partial quotients in the
continued-fraction expansion of `p/q`. Equivalently, the graph distance in the Farey /
tangency graph is computed by the continued-fraction algorithm.

*The key insight is* that a single mediant step is exactly one subtraction in the slow
(subtractive) Euclidean algorithm, so a chain of tangent circles is a geometric picture
of a continued fraction.

*Why now?* With mediants proved to preserve unimodularity and coprimality, the mediant
tree is a well-defined combinatorial object whose metric can be compared, term by term,
against the Euclidean algorithm on the same inputs.

## 4. Rigidity: tangency forces the radius law

**Conjecture.** Up to a global similarity, the assignment "cusp `p/q` ↦ circle of radius
`1/(2q²)` tangent to the axis at `p/q`" is the *unique* family of axis-tangent circles
for which every unimodular pair is tangent and no pair overlaps.

*The key insight is* that the gap identity forces the product of radii of any tangent
pair to equal a fixed multiple of `1/(q²s²)`; imposing this for all Farey neighbours
pins down each radius as a function of the denominator alone.

*Why now?* The gap identity proved here gives an exact algebraic constraint linking radii
to denominators, converting a vague geometric "why `1/(2q²)`?" into a solvable functional
equation over the Farey graph.

## 5. Signed determinants and a two-coloring of the tessellation

**Conjecture.** Orienting each tangency by the sign of `ps − qr` two-colors the edges of
the Farey graph consistently, and this coloring is preserved by the orientation-preserving
modular subgroup but flipped by orientation-reversing symmetries.

*The key insight is* that our invariance theorem preserves the determinant *with its
sign*, not merely its absolute value, so the sign carries real orientation data rather
than being a bookkeeping artifact.

*Why now?* Having proved the *signed* determinant (not just `|ps − qr|`) is conserved, we
can finally attach a meaningful parity/orientation to each edge and test whether it
organizes the tessellation into a bipartite-like structure.

import Mathlib

/-!
# The Library of Babel — foundations and the window probability

Borges' Library of Babel contains *every* book of a fixed length over a fixed
alphabet.  We formalise a book with alphabet size `b` and page count `L` as an
element of `Book b L := Fin L → Fin b`; the whole Library is the (finite) type
`Book b L`, of cardinality `b ^ L`.

## Main results

* `card_library` : the Library has exactly `b ^ L` volumes.
* `card_books_with_prefix` : the number of volumes whose first `m` pages spell a
  fixed word `T` is `b ^ (L - m)`.  Dividing by `b ^ L`, the probability that a
  uniformly random volume opens with `T` is `b ^ (-m)` — the exact "probability
  of finding a given proof-prefix in the Library".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the probability that a random volume contains a fixed
  target string `T` of length `m` in a fixed window is `b^{-m}`, independent of
  the enormous total length `L`.  Counter-intuitive because it says the Library's
  size is irrelevant to local content probability.
Experiment: brute-forced small cases (`b∈{2,3}`, `L≤4`); the count of prefix-`T`
  books is always `b^{L-m}` (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`).
Analysis: the statement is "true but needs the right definition": counting a
  `filter` over `Fin`-indexed windows is awkward, so we phrase it as the
  cardinality of a *subtype* (the fibre of the restriction map) and evaluate it
  by an explicit product equivalence `Book b L ≃ Book b m × Book b (L-m)`.
Critique: the prefix window is a faithful special case of "contains `T`"; the
  general substring count is `(L-m+1)` windows, quoted in the docstring, but the
  windows overlap so we only claim the clean per-window count here.
Synthesis: `card_books_with_prefix`, the arithmetic core of the probability
  conjecture, proved with 0 sorries.
-/

namespace LibraryOfBabel

/-- A *book* in the Library of Babel with alphabet size `b` and `L` pages:
a string of length `L` over the alphabet `Fin b`. -/
abbrev Book (b L : ℕ) : Type := Fin L → Fin b

/-- **Borges' count.** The Library of Babel with alphabet size `b` and page
count `L` contains exactly `b ^ L` distinct volumes. -/
theorem card_library (b L : ℕ) : Fintype.card (Book b L) = b ^ L := by
  simp [Book]

/-- The restriction of a book to its first `m` pages (`m ≤ L`). -/
def prefixWord {b L m : ℕ} (hmL : m ≤ L) (f : Book b L) : Book b m :=
  fun j => f (Fin.castLE hmL j)

/-
**Window probability (arithmetic core).**  The number of volumes whose first
`m` pages spell a fixed word `T` is `b ^ (L - m)`.  Hence the probability that a
uniformly random volume opens with `T` is `b ^ (L - m) / b ^ L = b ^ (-m)`.
-/
theorem card_books_with_prefix (b L m : ℕ) (hmL : m ≤ L) (T : Book b m) :
    Fintype.card {f : Book b L // prefixWord hmL f = T} = b ^ (L - m) := by
  rw [ Fintype.card_subtype ];
  -- We'll use the fact that if the prefix of a book is fixed, then the remaining part of the book can be any sequence of length $L - m$.
  have h_bij : {f : Book b L | prefixWord hmL f = T} ≃ (Fin (L - m) → Fin b) := by
    refine' Equiv.ofBijective ( fun f => fun i => f.val ⟨ m + i, by omega ⟩ ) ⟨ fun a b h => _, fun a => _ ⟩;
    · ext ⟨ i, hi ⟩ ; by_cases hi' : i < m <;> simp_all +decide [ funext_iff, Fin.ext_iff ];
      · convert congr_arg Fin.val ( congr_fun a.2 ⟨ i, hi' ⟩ ) using 1;
        exact congr_arg Fin.val ( congr_fun b.2 ⟨ i, hi' ⟩ ) ▸ rfl;
      · convert h ⟨ i - m, by omega ⟩ using 1 <;> simp +decide [ Nat.add_sub_of_le hi' ];
    · refine' ⟨ ⟨ fun i => if h : i.val < m then T ⟨ i.val, h ⟩ else a ⟨ i.val - m, by omega ⟩, _ ⟩, _ ⟩ <;> simp +decide [ funext_iff ];
      unfold prefixWord; aesop;
  convert Fintype.card_congr h_bij using 1;
  · rw [ Fintype.card_of_subtype ] ; aesop;
  · norm_num

end LibraryOfBabel

/-!
# The Library of Babel — the catalog dilemma

Does the Library contain its own complete catalog?  A *complete meaning-catalog*
is an assignment `Book b L → Bool` marking each volume (say, as meaningful or
not).

## Main results

* `no_single_universal_catalog` : **no single volume can encode the complete
  catalog** — a Cantor/diagonal argument.  There are `2 ^ (b^L)` catalogs but
  only `b^L` volumes, and `b^L < 2^(b^L)` always, so no map `Book → (Book → Bool)`
  is surjective.
* `distributed_catalog_exists` : a *distributed* catalog spread over a shelf of
  `N` volumes **can** encode every complete catalog, provided the shelf has
  enough capacity `2 ^ (b^L) ≤ b ^ (L*N)` — i.e. `N ≥ b^L / (L·log₂ b)`.

## Application (uses the catalog's Singleton bound)

* `robust_catalog_bound` : an error-correcting catalog (a set of volumes pairwise
  at Hamming distance `≥ d`) has at most `b ^ (L - (d-1))` entries.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): (B) one volume can never index the whole Library;
  (C) but `N` volumes can, once total capacity beats total information.
Experiment: `2^(b^L)` vs `b^L` for small `b,L` confirms `b^L < 2^(b^L)`; the
  threshold `2^(b^L) ≤ b^{L·N}` reproduces `N ≥ b^L/(L log₂ b)` numerically
  (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`).
Analysis: (B) is a clean pigeonhole once phrased with `Fintype.card_le_of_surjective`
  and `Nat.lt_two_pow_self`; no size hypothesis is needed.  (C) is
  `Function.Embedding.nonempty_of_card_le` once both cardinalities are computed
  (`card_fun`, `pow_mul`).
Critique: neither theorem is vacuous — (B) rules out a genuine surjection and (C)
  produces a genuine embedding; the capacity hypothesis of (C) is exactly the
  Borges threshold, not a hidden falsehood.  We additionally guard against
  triviality by tying the results to the concrete `Book` type and to the
  catalog's `SingletonBound.singleton_bound`.
Synthesis: (B), (C), and the robust-catalog corollary, all with 0 sorries.
-/

open Function

namespace LibraryOfBabel

/-
**No single universal catalog (diagonal argument).**  There is no volume
whose contents encode the complete meaning-catalog of the Library: no map from
volumes to complete catalogs `Book b L → Bool` can be surjective, because there
are strictly more catalogs (`2 ^ (b^L)`) than volumes (`b^L`).
-/
theorem no_single_universal_catalog (b L : ℕ) :
    ¬ ∃ decode : Book b L → (Book b L → Bool), Surjective decode := by
  by_contra h;
  convert Fintype.card_le_of_surjective _ h.choose_spec;
  simp +decide [ Fintype.card_pi ];
  exact Nat.lt_two_pow_self

/-
**Distributed catalog suffices.**  If a shelf of `N` volumes has capacity at
least the number of complete catalogs (`2 ^ (b^L) ≤ b ^ (L*N)`, equivalently
`N ≥ b^L / (L·log₂ b)`), then every complete catalog `Book b L → Bool` can be
encoded by such a shelf: there is an injection from catalogs to shelves.
-/
theorem distributed_catalog_exists (b L N : ℕ) (h : 2 ^ (b ^ L) ≤ b ^ (L * N)) :
    Nonempty ((Book b L → Bool) ↪ (Fin N → Book b L)) := by
  refine' Function.Embedding.nonempty_of_card_le _;
  simp +decide [ Fintype.card_pi ];
  rwa [ pow_mul ] at h

/-
**Robust catalog bound (application of the Singleton bound).**  A catalog
whose entries are pairwise at Hamming distance at least `d` — so each address
survives up to `⌊(d-1)/2⌋` corrupted symbols — contains at most `b ^ (L - (d-1))`
volumes.
-/
theorem robust_catalog_bound (b L d : ℕ) (hdL : d - 1 ≤ L)
    (C : Finset (Book b L)) (hsep : SingletonBound.Separated C d) :
    C.card ≤ b ^ (L - (d - 1)) := by
  convert SingletonBound.singleton_bound _ _;
  all_goals try infer_instance;
  · norm_num;
  · norm_num;
  · aesop;
  · assumption

end LibraryOfBabel

# Computational Evidence — The Library of Babel

We model the Library as `Book b L := Fin L → Fin b` (all strings of length `L`
over a `b`-symbol alphabet). The real Library is `b = 25`, `L = 1312000`.

## 1. Library size

`|Book b L| = b ^ L`. For the real Library this is `25 ^ 1312000`, the Borges count.

## 2. Prefix / window probability (Theorem A)

Number of books whose first `m` pages equal a fixed word `T` of length `m`:

| b | L | m | #books with prefix T | total b^L | ratio |
|---|---|---|----------------------|-----------|-------|
| 2 | 3 | 2 | 2  = 2^(3-2)          | 8         | 1/4 = 2^-2 |
| 2 | 4 | 2 | 4  = 2^(4-2)         | 16        | 1/4 = 2^-2 |
| 3 | 4 | 2 | 9  = 3^(4-2)         | 81        | 1/9 = 3^-2 |
| 25| L | m | 25^(L-m)             | 25^L      | 25^-m |

So the probability a uniformly random book opens with a target proof-string of
length `m` is exactly `b^{-m}`, matching the conjectured `|T|·25^{-k}` shape
(here the per-window probability `25^{-m}`; multiply by the `L-m+1` windows for
the expected occurrence count).

**Exact probability of a specific Lean-proof prefix of length `m` in the real
Library: `25^{-m}`.**

## 3. No single universal catalog (Theorem B — diagonal/Cantor)

A "complete meaning-catalog" is a function `Book b L → Bool` (mark each volume
meaningful or not). There are `2^(b^L)` such catalogs but only `b^L` books, and
`b^L < 2^(b^L)` always (`Nat.lt_two_pow_self`). Hence no surjection
`Book → (Book → Bool)`: no single book can encode the complete catalog.

| b | L | books b^L | catalogs 2^(b^L) |
|---|---|-----------|-------------------|
| 2 | 1 | 2         | 4                 |
| 2 | 2 | 4         | 16                |
| 2 | 3 | 8         | 256               |

## 4. Distributed catalog threshold (Theorem C)

A shelf of `N` books has `(b^L)^N = b^{L·N}` possible contents. It can store any
catalog `Book → Bool` iff `2^(b^L) ≤ b^{L·N}`, i.e. (taking `log_2`)
`b^L ≤ L·N·log_2 b`, i.e. `N ≥ b^L / (L·log_2 b)` — exactly the Borges
distributed-catalog threshold.

| b | L | b^L | need 2^(b^L) ≤ 2^(L·N) → N ≥ | threshold b^L/(L log2 b) |
|---|---|-----|------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 2 | 2 | 4   | N ≥ 2                        | 4/(2·1) = 2              |
| 2 | 3 | 8   | 2^8 ≤ 2^{3N} → N ≥ 3 (⌈8/3⌉) | 8/(3·1) ≈ 2.67 → 3       |

## 5. Robust catalog bound (application of the catalog's Singleton bound)

An error-correcting catalog (a set of books pairwise Hamming-distance ≥ `d`, so
each address survives up to `⌊(d-1)/2⌋` symbol corruptions) has size at most
`b^{L-d+1}` — the Singleton bound specialised to the Library.

All four numeric families above are reproduced exactly by the formalised theorems.

# Future Directions — Combinatorics of the Universal Library

The universal library — the space of *all* strings of a fixed length over a fixed
alphabet — turns "everything that can be written" into a finite combinatorial
object. This cycle established three anchors: the probability of a given opening
passage is independent of the library's overwhelming size; no single volume can
index the whole collection; but a shelf of volumes can, exactly when its total
capacity crosses an explicit information threshold. The following conjectures push
each anchor further.

## 1. Overlap-corrected occurrence law

**Conjecture.** For a target passage of length `m` drawn over a `b`-symbol
alphabet, the expected number of times it appears as a (possibly overlapping)
block inside a random volume of length `L` is exactly `(L - m + 1)·b^{-m}`, and
the *variance* is governed by the passage's autocorrelation polynomial: passages
with no nontrivial self-overlap (e.g. `ab...` with distinct symbols) are the most
sharply concentrated, while self-similar passages (e.g. `aaaa`) fluctuate most.

**The key insight is** that overlap structure, not passage length alone, controls
how reliably meaning recurs: a phrase that cannot overlap itself behaves like a
sequence of independent trials, whereas a self-echoing phrase clumps.

**Why now?** The single-window probability `b^{-m}` is now pinned down exactly;
the natural next step is to replace the crude union bound over the `L - m + 1`
windows by the precise second moment, which the autocorrelation polynomial makes
tractable.

## 2. The capacity threshold is sharp in both directions

**Conjecture.** A shelf of `N` volumes can encode every complete catalog of an
`L`-page, `b`-symbol library **iff** `N·L·log₂ b ≥ b^{L}`; that is, the sufficiency
bound `N ≥ b^{L}/(L·log₂ b)` is also *necessary* — one volume short of the
threshold, some catalog is provably unencodable, by a counting/pigeonhole
converse.

**The key insight is** that the library's storage problem is governed by a single
scalar — total symbol capacity versus total catalog entropy — so the threshold
cannot be beaten by any clever encoding, only met.

**Why now?** We have the sufficiency direction (enough capacity yields an
encoding). The counting argument that produced the diagonal impossibility for a
single volume generalizes verbatim to give the matching lower bound for shelves.

## 3. A de Bruijn master-index for the mini-library

**Conjecture.** For every alphabet size `b` and page count `L`, there is a single
cyclic super-string of length `b^{L}` in which every one of the `b^{L}` volumes
appears exactly once as a length-`L` window; consequently the entire library can
be *linearly ordered and addressed* by position along one cyclic sequence,
constructible in time polynomial in the library's size. The mini-library with
`b = 4`, `L = 16` is the smallest case combining a nontrivial alphabet with a
book length that already exceeds direct enumeration.

**The key insight is** that a master-index need not list volumes at all: a de
Bruijn cycle *is* the catalog, because consecutive windows walk through every
volume without repetition, turning "find volume `x`" into "find the offset of a
window equal to `x`".

**Why now?** The impossibility of a single indexing *volume* (item, this cycle)
sharpens the question of what a single indexing *sequence* can do; de Bruijn
cycles are exactly the objects that dodge the diagonal obstruction by living one
dimension up, in the shift space rather than in a single book.

## 4. Robust catalogs pay a length tax equal to their error tolerance

**Conjecture.** Among catalogs whose addresses survive up to `t` corrupted
symbols, the largest possible catalog has exactly `b^{L - 2t}` entries, and this
maximum is attained by a maximum-distance-separable family; equivalently, each
unit of error tolerance costs exactly two pages of addressable capacity.

**The key insight is** that error tolerance and addressable capacity are dual
resources trading off at a fixed exchange rate `2` (pages per unit of tolerance),
so a librarian's only real design choice is where to sit on this single tradeoff
line.

**Why now?** The Singleton-type upper bound `b^{L-d+1}` for distance-`d` catalogs
is in hand; the open half is *attainability* — exhibiting families that meet it —
which is precisely the classical maximum-distance-separable construction awaiting
transfer into the library setting.
